pr_title: kube-proxy: respect cluster cidr, do not drop packets from external cidr ranges if cluster cidr set
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
When kube-proxy is configured with a cluster-cidr range, it drops packets with an INVALID conntrack state for all sources on the KUBE-FORWARD chain. This is meant to prevent spurious retransmits in long-lived TCP connections to a service IP, but it prevents clusters from having asymmetrical routing on private subnets with services outside of a cluster.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #94861

**Special notes for your reviewer**:
None

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
```release-note
NONE
```

**Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.**:
```docs

```

issue_context.title: kube-proxy: Drop packets in INVALID state drops packets from outside the pod range
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:
When kube-proxy is configured with a cluster-cidr range, it drops packets with an INVALID conntrack state for all sources on the KUBE-FORWARD chain. This is meant to prevent spurious retransmits in long-lived TCP connections to a service IP, but it prevents clusters from having asymmetrical routing on private subnets with services outside of a cluster. 

**What you expected to happen**:
Packets on the KUBE-FORWARD chain with an INVALID conntrack state should be dropped for only sources inside of the cluster-cidr if set.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
N/A

**Anything else we need to know?**:
Change to drop INVALID conntrack packets was in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/74840. Backing out that commit and compiling is my current workaround.

@thockin I can try to give a bit more context to our setup, but the knowledge I have around this all dates back to Feb, unfortuately, so I may have forgotten details.

We were replacing our mesos cluster with a kubernetes cluster in Feb and using a custom ingress solution (HAProxy w/an outside process configuring it for pod ips / mesos ip-ports) for both. The ingress nodes lived in the private subnet, but outside of the kubernetes cluster cidr range. When we upgraded from kubernetes 1.14 to kubernetes 1.15 (the first version with PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/74840) our ingress could no longer talk to any pod ips. I discovered that the KUBE-FORWARD chain had a rule to drop invalid packets, which was added in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/74840. Compiling kubernetes 1.15 without this commit fixed our problems, and we have been carrying that patch forward ever since. I would like to get rid of our forked kubernetes, hence this ticket.

When I was writing this ticket up, I also found [a blog post](https://www.growse.com/2020/01/23/adventures-with-asymmetric-routing-and-firewalls.html) also mentions the same issue with the iptables dropping INVALID conntrack state packets near the end, regarding asymmetrical routing.

>Edit, OK I get the original problem, but still don't understand why packets from outside the pod range would not exhibit #74839, thereby requiring yet another revisit of this problem.

I think you are correct, I can imagine packets from outside of a cluster could exhibit the same behavior as packets inside the cluster and cause spurious resets. However, I  am wondering if kube-proxy should be managing packets from outside of the cluster on a node... That seems outside of the scope of kube-proxy.

I think the patch in #95197 is wrong; it changes the rule from "if INVALID then drop" to "if INVALID and _from a pod_, then drop" so that it doesn't affect non-kubernetes traffic, but I think the rule we actually need is "if INVALID and _to a service_, then drop". In particular, I believe we need to make sure that the rule applies to traffic with a cluster-external source and an in-cluster destination.

It's possible that changing it to "if INVALID and _to a pod_, then drop" would also work. I skimmed #74839 and some linked bugs elsewhere but I was unable to confirm whether that rule would cover the reporters' use cases.

For kube-proxy, this is done by the `LocalTrafficDetector`. If you are in a cluster where there is no simple way to discriminate pod from non-pod traffic, then you'd have to run kube-proxy with `--detect-local-mode ""`, and then kube-proxy will see that `proxier.localDetector.IsImplemented()` returns `false` and so it won't try to distinguish local from non-local traffic, and will do some things (like internal/external traffic policy) slightly differently as a result.

I did not understand how you could get asymmetric routing in K8s, but reading up more carefully I saw:

> using a custom ingress solution (HAProxy w/an outside process configuring it for pod ips / mesos ip-ports) for both

If I understand this correctly, this is a load-balancer outside K8s that load-balance directly to POD addresses. To get asymmetric routing some kind of Direct Server Return (DSR) must also be used. So, to get asymmetric routing:

1. Traffic from an external source is directed to an external LB
2. The LB is configured with POD-IPs as targets and selects one
3. The packet is routed to a K8s node, e.g. with ECMP. But is may not be the node where the target POD is executing
4. The packet is handled by the POD, but the response packet may be directed to some other GW

This will give asymmetric routing. But it's not the every-day K8s network setup for sure.

Given the above it's _fairly_ easy to reproduce the problem. You don't even have to setup a load-balancer. The biggest problem may be that you need two ways in to the cluster. Example:

![net-setup](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/37046727/69b8770d-cf68-49a2-a1cf-968c3e06d6d6)

I setup direct routes that ensures asymmetric routing, which can be checked with `tcpdump` on vm-201 and vm-202. From `vm-221` I can now directly ping POD-IPs, but due to the problem in this issue, I can't make a TCP connection:

```
vm-221 ~ # ping -c1 11.0.1.2
PING 11.0.1.2 (11.0.1.2) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 11.0.1.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=1.42 ms

--- 11.0.1.2 ping statistics ---
1 packets transmitted, 1 received, 0% packet loss, time 0ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 1.416/1.416/1.416/0.000 ms
vm-221 ~ # nc 11.0.1.2 5001
(hangs...)
```
The POD with address `11.0.1.2` runs on `vm-001`.

A similar setup as above can be used to verify a PR.

**Now, there is a simple work-around: use proxy-mode=ipvs**

The update with the `DROP` rule never made it to the ipvs proxier (a rather common case :cry: ), but in this case it may save your day. The same as above with proxy-mode=ipvs;

```
vm-221 ~ # ping -c1 11.0.1.2
PING 11.0.1.2 (11.0.1.2) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 11.0.1.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=2.27 ms

--- 11.0.1.2 ping statistics ---
1 packets transmitted, 1 received, 0% packet loss, time 0ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 2.273/2.273/2.273/0.000 ms
vm-221 ~ # nc 11.0.1.2 5001
tserver-55b644d88b-5lsq5
```
The server on 5001 responds with the POD name.

> Now, there is a simple work-around: use proxy-mode=ipvs

Yeah, Our production environment also solved this problem by switching to IPVS mode. In IPVS mode, there is no _the DROP rule_.
